Machinist Assistant v1.0.0

Offline calculation and reference helper for industrial machinists: turning, milling, drilling and tapping calculators, unit converter, part weight, metric threads, cutting speeds, ISO fits and drill charts.

Suggested values are workshop guidelines. Always confirm with your machine and tooling datasheets.
Typical fz for this material: %s mm
Deep hole (L greater than 3×D): use peck drilling and retract the chips.
Tapping Vc is reduced to 60 percent of drilling. On CNC use a floating tap holder.
Vc values are in m/min for turning. Reduce 20 to 30 percent for drilling and milling.
Tolerances are in micrometers (µm) per ISO 286, hole-basis fits with H7/H8.\nExample 25H7/g6: hole 25 0/+0.021, shaft 25 −0.007/−0.020.
Start from the cutting speed table, then adjust by chip color, tool wear and vibration. These formulas are the backbone of every machining calculation in this app.

string-array.name: guide_items
string-array.item:
1. Cutting speed Vc
Vc = π × D × N / 1000

Cutting speed is the surface speed of the cutting edge in m/min. Higher Vc means higher productivity but faster tool wear. Always start from the cutting speed table, then tune by chip color, edge wear, vibration and surface finish. Blue or dark chips on steel usually mean Vc is too high for the insert grade.

2. Spindle speed N
N = (1000 × Vc) / (π × D)

Bigger diameter means lower RPM for the same Vc. Example: Vc = 110 m/min on D = 50 mm gives N ≈ 700 rpm. On a conventional lathe, set the closest lower RPM the gearbox offers.

3. Feed
Turning: Vf = f × N
Milling: Vf = fz × Z × N

Feed is the tool advance per revolution (turning) or per tooth (milling). Too low a feed on stainless steel rubs the edge and work-hardens the surface; too high a feed increases cutting force and risks edge chipping. Roughing typically uses 2 to 3 times the finishing feed.

4. Material removal rate
Turning: Q = Vc × f × ap (cm³/min)
Milling: Q = ap × ae × Vf / 1000 (cm³/min)

Q tells how fast metal is removed and how much power is needed. Keep Q within the available spindle and motor power of the machine.

5. Cutting power
Pc = kc × ap × f × Vc / 60000 (kW)
Motor power = Pc / η

kc is the specific cutting force of the material in N/mm² (see the speeds table data used by the calculators). η is drive efficiency, typically 75 to 85 percent on older machines. If Pc exceeds 80 percent of available motor power, reduce ap or f.

6. Tap drill size
Tap drill = D − P

D is the thread nominal diameter and P is the pitch. Example M8 × 1.25 → 8 − 1.25 = 6.75, use a 6.8 mm drill. In soft material you can go 0.1 mm larger to reduce tapping torque.

7. Machining time
Turning: T = L / (f × N)
Drilling: T = (L + 0.3×D) / (f × N)
Milling: T = (L + lc) / Vf with lc = √(ae × (Dc − ae))

Add approach and overtravel allowances when quoting cycle time. For deep holes (L greater than 3×D) plan peck drilling which increases real time.

8. Workshop tips
• Roughing: large ap, medium f, then finishing pass with small f for surface finish.
• Vibration or chatter: reduce Vc or ap first, then increase feed slightly.
• Use cutting fluid on steels and stainless; dry machining suits cast iron and many carbide inserts.
• Constant chip shape means stable process; long stringy chips mean change feed or use chip breaker geometry.
